title: US Midterms May Shift Market Sentiment, but Analysts See No Sustained Trend Reversal
excerpt: With inflation at 3.7% and the Fed raising rates again, analysts quoted by Moneycontrol and asset managers say earnings, oil and the rate path, not the November 3 result, will set the market's direction.
body:
• Analysts quoted in Moneycontrol's Daily Voice and other market research say the November 3 US midterms may shift sentiment, but a sustained trend reversal is unlikely while inflation and Federal Reserve policy dominate returns.
  • US inflation is running at 3.7%, well above the Fed's 2% target, and the Fed raised its policy rate in September to 3.75%-4.00%; the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34%, its highest since 2002.
  • Prediction markets price a strong Democratic House outcome: Kalshi gives Democrats a 91% chance of reclaiming the House, while BCA Research puts the chance of a Democratic Senate at 60%.
  • History favours stocks after the vote: JPMorgan data show the S&P 500 averaging about a 15% gain in the 12 months after midterms since 1950, though midterm years themselves have averaged 7.5% against 12.4% for all years, according to Morningstar.

The US midterm elections on November 3 could move market sentiment in the short term, but they are unlikely to reverse the market's underlying trend. That is the assessment in Moneycontrol's Daily Voice column and in research from asset managers ahead of the vote: inflation, oil prices and the Federal Reserve's rate path remain the forces that set equity returns, ahead of the composition of Congress.

All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are in play. Polling averages give Democrats a lead of about nine points on the generic congressional ballot, and markets broadly expect a divided Congress from January, according to Wright Research's analysis of the vote. Prediction markets are more emphatic: Kalshi prices a 91% probability of a Democratic majority in the House, and BCA Research assigns a 60% chance of Democrats winning the Senate.

Inflation outweighs the election

The numbers explain the caution. US headline inflation rose to 3.7% in September, with energy prices up about 20% from a year earlier. Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said companies create value through profits rather than election results, and he does not expect the midterms to have a meaningful impact on markets. The analyst quoted in the Daily Voice column, Bivalkar, likewise identified inflation trends as the dominant influence, while flagging telecom as a potential cash generator if investment intensity falls and pricing discipline holds.

Consumer data point the same way. The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index fell to 48.0 in October, the second-lowest reading on record, as households focused on purchasing power ahead of the vote, Reuters reported. The Conference Board's consumer confidence index fell to 81.9 in September, its lowest since 2014.

The rate channel is what reaches portfolios

For investors, the election matters mainly through interest rates. The Federal Reserve raised its policy rate in September to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, its first increase since 2023, and markets expect at least one more hike by December. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34% in late September, the highest since 2002. A divided Congress tends to slow new spending and ease pressure on Treasury supply; a Republican sweep would make further tax cuts and defence spending more likely, adding to issuance at yields investors already find demanding.

The sector most exposed to the result is technology. Keith Lerner, chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services, noted that a Democratic-controlled Congress might oppose the development of data centres, the infrastructure behind the AI build-out that has driven recent market gains. Credit markets are already signalling strain there: the cost of insuring the debt of Oracle and CoreWeave against default has risen to its highest since the AI spending cycle began in 2023.

What history says, and its limits

The historical pattern is favourable after election day, not before it. Morningstar data show the S&P 500 averaging 7.5% in midterm years against 12.4% across all years, with declines of 18.1% in 2022 and 4.4% in 2018. JPMorgan research finds the index has posted positive returns in the 12 months following every midterm since 1950, averaging about 15%. Wright Research puts the equivalent figure at about 14%, with gains after 32 of the last 38 midterms, while noting analysts at U.S. Bank regard the pattern as statistically weak next to the economy's influence.

The India transmission

The vote reaches Indian markets through the dollar and US yields rather than through politics directly. Foreign investors have sold a record Rs 3.04 lakh crore of Indian equities in 2026, the Nifty is down about 14% this year and the rupee has lost close to 7% against the dollar. The Reserve Bank of India raised its repo rate on October 7 to 5.50%, its first increase since February 2023. A midterm outcome that pressures the Fed to pause would reduce the pull of US yields and could return some foreign capital to India; continued yield rises would keep the RBI defending the rupee and Indian equities under pressure.

What to watch

The sequence that matters is the result on November 3, then the Fed's December decision and the path of the 10-year Treasury yield. On the evidence analysts are publishing, investors pricing a structural reversal on the election alone are trading the wrong variable: earnings, oil and the inflation print will decide the trend, and the midterms will decide, at most, the sentiment around it.
